Hook: Some time in the 1960s, an economist was driving to Columbia University in New York, late for the oral examination of a student in economic theory. Columbia had no parking for its teachers. He had two choices. A car park, which cost money for certain. Or the street, which was illegal and free, unless a warden came by and wrote a ticket. There was no time to think about it for long. He weighed the chance of a ticket, the size of the fine, and the price of the car park, and parked in the street. He was not ticketed. The economist was Gary Becker. On the walk to the examination room, he said later, it occurred to him that the city had probably made a similar calculation, in deciding how often to check the cars and how large to make the fine. His paper, Crime and Punishment: An Economic Approach, appeared in 1968.

The arithmetic is short. Park in the street if the chance of a ticket times the fine is less than the price of the car park. Say a warden comes one day in ten and the fine is thirty dollars: an expected cost of three dollars. If the car park costs five, the street is cheaper, for anyone who does not mind the risk. Becker's claim was that the same arithmetic, the gain from an act against the chance and size of a penalty, applies to theft, to cheating on taxes and to speeding, and that most offenders are not different kinds of people, just people facing different prices.

Becker spent the next thirty years applying the model of choice under constraint to things economists had left to others, and won the Nobel prize for it in 1992. This part's question: how far can that model be pushed into the rest of life? To crime: do penalties deter, and how would we know? To the family: the use of time, marriage, how many children and who decides. To schools and health. And to addiction, where the model is most strained, and where its critics say it breaks.
Economics, Built. Part forty-nine: the economic approach.

Here is the plan. Crime as a choice, a deterrent chosen by you, and what happens when economists try to measure whether police reduce crime. The household as a small factory, marriage as a market, the number of children, and bargaining between husband and wife. Schools, on the data from Tennessee's class-size experiment, teachers, and early childhood. Health, drugs and addiction, and the critics of the whole enterprise. Three dials, the people who use these ideas, and the frontier.
Crime: Chapter one. Crime as a choice.

Here is Becker's model on the Island. Twenty thousand potential offenders, each with a gain from some offence, measured in the years of prison it would be worth to them. Most gains are small; a few are large. The police catch one offender in five, and the sentence is 3 years. Someone who does not mind risk offends when the gain beats the expected punishment, the chance times the sentence: 0.6 years. Here, 73 percent of them would. Raise either the chance or the sentence and the line moves right: fewer offend. The supply of offences, like any supply, slopes.

Becker's second question was the city's: what is the cheapest way to deter? For an offender who does not mind risk, only the product of the chance and the fine matters. Every point on this curve deters exactly as much. But the points do not cost the same. Catching people takes police, courts and time; a fine, once someone is caught, costs almost nothing: money moves from one pocket to another. So slide along the curve: a bigger fine, a smaller chance, the same deterrence, less spent on catching. The slide stops only at the largest fine anyone can pay. Becker's answer: fines as large as possible, enforcement as thin as possible. On the Island, with each offence doing harm worth two years, the best plan is a fine of 40 and a chance of 12 percent, and only 2.5 percent offend.

No country hangs parking offenders, and the model says why not, once it is filled in. Fines are capped by what people have; beyond that the penalty must be prison, which costs the state money and the prisoner years, and is no longer a mere transfer. George Stigler added marginal deterrence: if robbery and murder carried the same penalty, a robber would lose nothing by killing the witness, so penalties must rise with the harm. Courts make mistakes, and a huge penalty applied rarely is also applied, sometimes, to the innocent. And the model so far assumed offenders who do not mind risk and count every future year of prison fully. Change that, and the answer to the simplest question changes. Which is the next chapter's game.
PlayIt: Chapter two. Play it: double the chance, or double the sentence?

Your turn. You run the Island's justice system, and you can afford one change. The police catch one offender in 5, and the sentence is 3 years. You may double the chance of being caught, by putting more police on the streets, or double the sentence, by passing a law. Either way the expected punishment, the chance times the sentence, doubles. Which cuts crime more: the chance, the sentence, or does it make no difference? Pause, and choose.

The answer depends on who the offenders are. For someone who weighs only the expected punishment, it makes no difference: either change cuts the share who offend from 73 to 40 percent. For someone who dislikes risk, the longer sentence deters more, because a small chance of a very long sentence is the more frightening gamble: 7 percent offend, against 24. For someone who counts each later year of prison for less than the one before, as most of us count the future, the extra years at the end of a longer sentence are far away and weigh little; doubling the chance, which brings the first years forward for twice as many, wins: 53 percent against 69. So the question is not one of theory. It has to be answered with data.

The data have answered fairly consistently. Daniel Nagin's review of the evidence concluded that the chance of being caught deters far more reliably than the severity of the punishment, and that long sentences cannot be justified as deterrents. David Lee and Justin McCrary used Florida's eighteenth birthday, when offenders suddenly face adult courts and much longer sentences. Offending barely changes: a fall of about 2 percent in the odds, ruling out falls of 11 percent or more. They put the response of young offenders to the length of a sentence at no more than minus 0.13. Becker had seen this coming: if the chance deters more than the penalty, offenders behave as if they like risk, or, as the Island's present-minded offenders show, as if the far end of a long sentence hardly counts.
Deterrence: Now the evidence. The obvious study compares places. Here are the Island's 1,000 city blocks, the police on each against its crime. The city, sensibly, sends police where it expects crime. So the blocks with the most police have the most crime: the slope is 0.75. Read naively, police cause crime. The truth planted in the Island is the opposite: each percent more police cuts crime by 0.3 percent. The comparison is ruined because police are not placed at random.

Three ways to estimate it. Comparing blocks: 0.75, the wrong sign. Following each block over time removes what is permanent about it, but changes in police from year to year are small, and police are counted with error. Here only 29 percent of the measured changes are real; the rest is noise, which drags the estimate toward zero: minus 0.08. Aaron Chalfin and Justin McCrary found exactly this in American cities' police counts. What works is moving police for a reason that has nothing to do with crime. Move them at random on the Island, and the estimate is minus 0.33, close to the truth. Nobody assigns police at random in a real city. But sometimes history does.

Two such accidents. In July 1994 a bomb destroyed the AMIA Jewish community centre in Buenos Aires and killed eighty-five people. The government put police outside every Jewish institution in the city, day and night, where they were placed by a threat of terror, not by the crime around them. Rafael Di Tella and Ernesto Schargrodsky counted car thefts: on the protected blocks they fell by 75 percent relative to other blocks. A block or two away, nothing changed: police deter where they stand. In July 2005, after the London bombings, police were moved into central London for weeks. Mirko Draca, Stephen Machin and Robert Witt found crime fell there relative to outer London, an elasticity of about minus 0.3 to minus 0.4: a tenth more police, three or four percent less crime. Close to the Island's planted value, which was chosen to match.

The hardest case is the most severe penalty. In 1975 Isaac Ehrlich estimated from American time series that each execution deterred several murders, and the study was quickly drawn into the American argument over the death penalty. Here are the 1950 data his critics used: murders per hundred thousand in forty-four states against executions per conviction. The southern states, in red, had both more executions and far more murder. Regress murder on executions and convictions alone, and executions seem to raise murder. Add region, income and race, and the estimate shrinks, with an error larger than itself. Edward Leamer and Walter McManus showed that, with data like these, the deterrent effect of execution can be made large, zero or negative by the choice of controls: the data cannot settle it. Their lesson, to report how an answer moves with the assumptions behind it, is one this series follows.
Family: Chapter four. The household as a small factory.

In 1965 Becker treated the household itself as a small factory. It buys goods with money earned at work, combines them with its own time at home, and produces what people actually want: meals, care, rest, the raising of children. Those commodities are what give utility. The idea has two consequences. A household's real budget is its full income, every hour valued at the wage, whether it is sold or not. And every commodity has a price that includes the time it takes. As wages rise, the commodities that take a lot of time, a home-cooked dinner, a large family, get dearer, and households shift toward those that take goods instead.

Here is an Island household of two adults. He earns more in the market; she is more productive at home, 1.67 times as productive, in the model. Who should do what? The answer is comparative advantage, the same as in trade between countries. While her wage is low, she specializes at home and he works for pay. As her wage rises, past about 0.70 of his, she starts paid work, and her share of time at work rises steadily. Nothing in the model says who should stay home; it is the ratio of wages to home skills that decides. Becker's critics pointed out that the home skills themselves are shaped by who was expected to stay home, and the model takes them as given.

The record of the twentieth century fits the model's direction. In America, 33 percent of women were in the labour force in 1948. The share rose for half a century, to 60 percent in 1999, and is 57 percent now. Men's fell, from 87 to 68, as they stayed longer in school and retired earlier. In Becker's terms, women's wages rose, machines made housework take less time, and families had fewer children, which made time at home worth less and time at work worth more. Claudia Goldin, who won the Nobel prize in 2023 for this history, added what the model leaves out: rules that barred married women from many jobs, norms that changed slowly, and, as chapter six shows, the pill, which let women plan careers.
Marriage: Chapter five. Marriage as a matching market.

In 1973 Becker treated marriage as a market in which men and women choose partners, and the gains from a match are shared. Suppose a couple's output, everything a household makes, depends on both partners' skills, and that the skills are complements: a high-skilled pair makes ten, a mixed pair six, a low-skilled pair three. Sorting, high with high and low with low, makes thirteen in all; mixing makes twelve. So the market sorts: like marries like, the same supermodularity that drove the stable matchings of Part seventeen. If instead traits substitute, as when one partner earns and the other keeps house, the market pairs opposites. Which is true is a question for data.

Here is the Island's marriage market. Men and women by schooling, school only, some college, or a degree, and the number of marriages between each pair of types, with those who stay single at the edges. The diagonal is heavy: like marries like, 1.41 times as often as if couples formed at random. Eugene Choo and Aloysius Siow showed in 2006 that counts like these reveal the gains from each kind of match. If tastes for particular partners vary at random, the number of marriages between two types, relative to the number who stay single on each side, grows with the joint surplus of that match. So the surplus of every pairing can be read off a census table.

Here is the check. On the left, the surplus of each kind of match planted in the Island: largest for two graduates, negative for a graduate and someone with school only. On the right, the surplus read back from one census of the Island's marriages, using only the counts. It is close, within the noise of a finite sample. Choo and Siow did this with American censuses, and found that the gains to marriage for young adults fell during the 1970s, partly as abortion became legal and the cost of a pregnancy outside marriage fell.

Because the model is an equilibrium, it can answer what-ifs. Give the Island a fifth more men in every group, as in countries where sons were preferred and daughters went unborn. The share of men who marry falls from 82 to 74 percent, and the share of women rises, from 78 to 85: the scarce side of a market does better. Or let women's schooling outrun men's, as it has in most rich countries, so that women with degrees far outnumber men with degrees. The share of graduate women who stay single rises from 22 to 27 percent. The frontier chapter returns to markets like these.
Fertility: Chapter six. Children: how many, and how much for each.

Why do richer families, and richer countries, have fewer children? Becker's answer, with Gregg Lewis, was that parents choose both how many children to have and how much to spend on each, their quality, in the economist's cold word. A child costs goods, and time, valued at the wage of the parent who gives it, most often the mother. As her wage rises, each child costs more, and the number of children falls, here from 5.5 to 1.4. Spending on each child rises. The two choices feed each other: spending more on each child makes another child dearer, since it too would get that spending, and fewer children make spending on each one cheaper. Small changes in wages can start a large shift, from many children with little each to few with much.

Here is the record. Children per woman since 1950: the world's average fell from 4.9 to 2.3. China is the famous case, because of its one-child policy of 1980. But look where China's line was by then. It had already fallen from 6.1 children in 1970 to 2.7 in 1979, during a campaign for later marriage, longer gaps and fewer children, and as incomes and schooling rose. Today it is 1.0. South Korea, which never had a one-child rule, is at 0.72, the lowest in the world. Japan and the United States are below replacement too. The policy surely mattered; but the fall that Becker's model predicts as women's time grows dearer went on everywhere, with or without it.

Do children reduce their mothers' work, or do women who plan to work less have more children? Joshua Angrist and William Evans found a lever chosen by nature. Here are 30,000 American mothers of at least two children in 1980. Parents of two boys or two girls are more likely to try for a third than parents of one of each: 40 and 42 percent against 34. And the sexes of the first two children are as good as random. So same-sex mothers had a third child 6.7 points more often, and worked 0.40 weeks less in 1979. Divide one by the other: a third child cut its mother's work by about 6 weeks a year. In this sample of thirty thousand the estimate is noisy, with a standard error of 3.8 weeks. With all a quarter of a million, Angrist and Evans found the effect real but smaller than the naive comparison suggests, and absent for more educated women.

One more lever changed the price of children. The pill, from the 1960s, put reliable contraception in women's hands. At first many states denied it to young unmarried women, until they lowered the age of majority, at different times. Claudia Goldin and Lawrence Katz used those differences. Where young single women could get the pill earlier, they married later and entered law and medical schools in larger numbers: careers that take years of training became safe to plan. In Becker's terms, a new technology lowered the cost of controlling the timing of children, and with it the cost of a career.
Bargaining: Chapter seven. Bargaining inside the household.

Becker's household made decisions as if it were one person, with one budget and one set of tastes. In this unitary household income is pooled: a pound earned by the father and a pound earned by the mother buy the same things. The alternative, developed by Pierre-André Chiappori, Shelly Lundberg, Robert Pollak and others, is a household of two people with their own tastes, who bargain. Each one's weight in the bargain rises with what they would have on their own, and so with the share of the income they control. Then who receives the money matters. That is testable.

On the Island, a household where the mother cares more than the father about spending on their child. In the unitary household, the share of the budget spent on the child is the same however the income is split. In the collective household it rises with the mother's share of the income, because her weight in the household's decisions rises with it. Now move a tenth of the household's income from the father's pay packet to the mother's purse, with total income unchanged. Spending on the child rises 13 percent. In the unitary model it would not change at all.

Britain ran the experiment. Until the late 1970s, most support for children came as a tax allowance, which raised the father's take-home pay. Then it was turned into a cash benefit, paid to the mother. Shelly Lundberg, Robert Pollak and Terence Wales found that spending on children's and women's clothing rose relative to spending on men's clothing. Income is not pooled. Studies since, of pensions paid to grandmothers in South Africa and of cash paid to mothers elsewhere, have mostly found similar patterns, one reason many transfer programmes now pay the mother.
Schools: Chapter eight. Schools: class size and teachers.

Schools are where the economic approach has been most argued over, because so much public money is at stake. Here are California's 420 elementary districts at the end of the 1990s, the textbook data of Stock and Watson: average test scores against the number of pupils per teacher. One more pupil per teacher goes with a score 2.28 points lower. But smaller classes are found in richer districts, with fewer children still learning English, and those children would score higher anyway. Allow for those two differences and the slope falls by more than half, to minus 1.00. Which differences have been missed? A comparison like this can never be sure. An experiment can.

In 1985 Tennessee ran one. Project STAR assigned 5,786 kindergarten pupils in 79 schools, and their teachers, at random to small classes of thirteen to seventeen, regular classes of twenty-two to twenty-five, or regular classes with a teacher's aide. Here are the scores at the end of kindergarten, reading and maths together, as percentiles of the regular classes: the small classes averaged 56.3, the others about 51. On the right, the gap at every rank, from the weakest pupils to the strongest: it is positive all the way along. Comparing pupils within the same school, small classes scored 5.6 percentile points higher, with a standard error of 1.4. The aides did nothing measurable. The gains were larger for poor children and for black children. Alan Krueger, analysing the same experiment, put the first year's gain at about four points, growing about a point a year after.

Israel has an older rule, from the twelfth-century scholar Maimonides: no more than forty pupils to a class. So a grade of forty is one class of forty, but a grade of forty-one is split into two classes of twenty or twenty-one. Class size falls off a cliff at each multiple of forty, for reasons that have nothing to do with the pupils. On the Island, where bigger schools are in richer towns, the naive slope of scores on class size is about zero. Comparing schools just either side of the cutoffs recovers the planted effect: minus 0.021 standard deviations per pupil. Joshua Angrist and Victor Lavy found gains from smaller classes in Israel's 1991 data. Returning with data from 2002 to 2011, Angrist, Lavy and colleagues found none, and found something else: too many schools enrolled just enough pupils to get the extra class. Where a rule pays, people learn to meet it.

Class size is one input; the teacher is another. On the Island, teachers differ in how much their pupils gain in a year. Estimate each teacher's effect from two years of classes and the estimates are too spread out, 0.16 against a true 0.12, because a class of twenty-five is a noisy measure. Shrink each estimate toward the average in proportion to its reliability, 0.62 here, and the spread is right. But are the estimates biased by which pupils a teacher gets? Raj Chetty, John Friedman and Jonah Rockoff tested this when teachers moved between schools: if the estimates are unbiased, a school's scores should change one for one with the predicted effect of the teachers who arrive and leave. On the Island the slope is 1.01. If schools' pupils differ and the estimates ignore it, the test catches it: the slope falls to 0.38. In real data the test passed, and they found that a teacher one standard deviation better raises scores by 0.14 standard deviations in maths and 0.10 in English, and earnings at twenty-eight by 1.3 percent.
Early: If schools matter, perhaps what comes before school matters more. In 1962, in Ypsilanti, Michigan, the Perry Preschool project took 123 three- and four-year-olds from poor black families, and gave about half of them, chosen roughly by lottery, two years of preschool and weekly home visits. They have been followed to the age of forty. The gains in test scores faded within a few years. But as adults the children who went earned more, were arrested less and depended less on welfare. James Heckman and colleagues estimated a return to society of 7 to 10 percent a year, better than the stock market's.

From Perry and a few similar programmes came an influential picture. James Heckman argued that skills beget skills: what a child learns early makes later learning cheaper, so the return to investing in people falls with the age at which it is made. The picture is drawn from theory and a handful of programmes; it is not a curve fitted to many. David Rea and Tony Burton took the benefit-cost ratios of hundreds of programmes evaluated for Washington State and found no sign that returns fall with the age of the people served: good and bad programmes at every age. Heckman replied that his curve was about what is possible, not about the average programme. Both can be true.

And when programmes like Perry are scaled up? Perry was small and intensive, run by enthusiasts and followed for decades. America's national Head Start programme was put to a randomized trial: the gains at the end of the programme had largely faded by the end of first grade, with few differences left by third. Its defenders point to long-run studies of Head Start that find gains in adulthood, as at Perry. Tennessee's statewide pre-kindergarten programme was also tested by lottery, with 2,990 children. By sixth grade, the children offered a place were doing worse than the others, with lower scores and more trouble at school. The lesson is not that early childhood does not matter. It is that a programme is not a category: what works at small scale with the best staff may not survive being scaled up.
Health: Chapter ten. The demand for health.

In 1972 Michael Grossman treated health as a stock of capital. People are born with some, it wears out, and they can invest in it, with doctors' visits, food, exercise and their own time. Its return is healthy days, for work and for life. It pays to hold health up to the point where the extra healthy days from one more unit equal what it costs to keep it: the interest forgone plus the rate at which it wears out. That rate rises with age, so the health it pays to keep falls, and when it would fall below the minimum for life, life ends: here at 86. People who are better at producing health, Grossman argued, as schooling makes them, choose more of it and live longer. In the model the death age is a choice, which is the model's most criticized feature, and its most provocative.

If health care is bought like other things, insurance that lowers its price should raise how much is used. Here are 5,190 adults from Australia's health survey of 1977 and 1978, with their doctor visits in two weeks, by the kind of cover they had. Those with free cover because of age or war service visit most, but they are also old and ill: a raw comparison mixes the price of care with the need for it. Holding illness, days of reduced activity, chronic conditions, age, sex and income equal, in a count regression, private cover goes with 13 percent more visits, but the interval runs from 6 percent fewer to 36 percent more: these data cannot pin it down. And people who expect to need care also buy cover, so even the estimate is not clean; that is why the RAND experiment of Part forty-two assigned cover at random.

Health care is also unlike other markets. Patients know little, and the doctor who advises them is also the one who is paid for the care. Jonathan Gruber and Maria Owings looked at America from 1970 to 1982, when births fell by 13.5 percent and obstetricians lost income. Where births fell most, caesarean sections, which pay more than natural deliveries, rose most. The effect was real but small: it explains little of the overall rise in caesareans. And hospitals with market power charge for it: Zack Cooper and colleagues found that American hospitals with no competitor nearby charge prices about 12 percent higher than those with four or more, the measurement of market power from Part forty-three applied to medicine.
Drugs: Chapter eleven. Drugs, patents and despair.

A new medicine is expensive to discover and cheap to make. On the Island, a course of a new drug costs 10 dollars to make. While the patent lasts, its owner charges the monopoly price, 55 dollars, and sells 45 thousand courses a year. The profit, 2.02 million dollars a year, is what pays for the research that found the drug, and for the failures along the way. The red triangle is the cost: patients who would have paid more than the cost of making the drug, but not the patent price, go without, 1.01 million dollars of value a year, until the patent runs out and generics bring the price down to the cost, and 90 thousand courses are sold. The patent trades that triangle now for medicines in the future; how long and how strong patents should be is a question of how much more research the profit calls forth.

In 2015 Anne Case and Angus Deaton found something that should not happen in a rich country. The death rate of white Americans aged forty-five to fifty-four, which had fallen for decades, rose from 1999 to 2013, while it kept falling in other rich countries. The causes were suicide, poisoning by drugs and alcohol, and liver disease: deaths of despair, they called them. Had the 1998 death rate held, about 96,000 deaths would have been avoided. Case and Deaton pointed to decades of worsening prospects for Americans without degrees. Others asked about supply: were the drugs themselves the cause?

Abby Alpert, William Evans, Ethan Lieber and David Powell found a natural experiment in supply. In 1996 Purdue Pharma launched OxyContin, a strong opioid, and marketed it hard. But 5 states required doctors to write prescriptions for such drugs on special triplicate forms, which left a trail for the authorities. Doctors there disliked the forms, and the company's own planning treated those states as hard markets. OxyContin's distribution was about 50 percent lower there, and their overdose deaths, once higher than elsewhere, grew more slowly, for twenty years. Had the other states been as little exposed, they estimate, they would have had 34 percent fewer drug overdose deaths and 45 percent fewer opioid overdose deaths a year. Despair may explain who was vulnerable; the supply of the drug explains much of who died.
Addiction: Addiction looks like the opposite of choice. In 1988 Becker and Kevin Murphy argued that it could be chosen anyway. Past use builds a stock, of tolerance and habit. The stock makes more use more rewarding now: this is what makes a good addictive. And it does harm later, to health, to work, to family. A rational addict, in their model, sees all of this and still chooses to use, because the pleasure now is worth the cost later to them. The model's sharpest prediction is about the future: if the price of a drug will rise next year, a rational addict cuts back now.

Two Island users of an addictive good, starting from nothing. The myopic one ignores how today's use will shape tomorrow's cravings and harms; use climbs as the habit builds. The rational one counts those effects, and settles at a lower level. At period 10, a price rise is announced, to take effect ten periods later. The myopic user carries on climbing, +23 percent before the rise. The rational user starts cutting back at once, 7 percent before the price has changed, because cutting back now leaves a smaller habit to feed when the price is high. When the rise comes, both cut sharply, and the rational addict's long-run response is the larger.

Do addicts respond to prices at all? Here are the forty-eight continental states in 1995, cigarettes smoked per head against the real price of a pack. Prices differ mostly because taxes differ. A simple regression gives an elasticity of minus 1.21. But price and consumption are set together, so use the general sales tax, which moves the price of cigarettes for reasons unrelated to smoking, as an instrument: minus 1.08. Over ten years, from 1985 to 1995, with both the sales tax and the tax on cigarettes as instruments: minus 1.20. These are the textbook estimates of Stock and Watson, reproduced here. Smokers are addicted, and smokers respond to price, about one for one in the long run. Both are true.

Jonathan Gruber and Botond Kőszegi put the sharpest prediction to the data. When cigarette tax rises were announced in advance, did smoking fall before they took effect? It did: smokers are forward-looking. But the same evidence fits smokers who are forward-looking and present-biased, like the gym members of Part forty-five, who plan to quit and keep putting it off. And the difference matters. For Becker's rational addict, a tax only costs the smoker. For the present-biased one, a tax helps them do what they themselves wanted to do, and the right tax is much higher. The model survives the test; its welfare advice does not, necessarily.
Critics: Chapter thirteen. Economics imperialism, and the reply.

By 2000, Edward Lazear could title a paper Economic Imperialism, and mean it as praise. Economics, he argued, had spread into the other social sciences because it had something they lacked: one model of rational choice, an equilibrium, and an insistence on what can be measured. So it travelled: to crime, the family, law, politics, even religion. The critics, sociologists, psychologists and many economists, answered that people are not moved by prices alone, but by duty, shame, identity and meaning. And they made a sharper claim, which can be tested: that putting a price on something can change what it is.

The most famous test is Uri Gneezy and Aldo Rustichini's. Ten day-care centres in the Israeli city of Haifa, where parents sometimes came late to collect their children and a teacher had to wait. For 4 weeks they counted the late parents. Then 6 of the centres introduced a small fine for arriving more than 10 minutes late. Becker's model says lateness should fall. It rose, and when the fine was removed some weeks later, it stayed up. The authors' reading: before the fine, lateness was a favour asked of a teacher, with some guilt attached. The fine made it a service with a price, and the price was low. The fine did not add to the cost of lateness; it replaced one cost with another, and the guilt did not come back.

In 1970 Richard Titmuss argued that paying for blood would drive out those who give it freely. Carl Mellström and Magnus Johannesson tested it in Sweden, asking people to become blood donors. Without payment, 52 percent of the women did. Offered 50 kronor, about seven dollars, only 30 percent did. For men, payment made no difference. And when the money could be given to charity instead, women's giving returned. Paying people to be generous made generosity look like work, for some of them.

There are more such findings. Bruno Frey and Felix Oberholzer-Gee found that Swiss residents' support for a nuclear waste site near them fell when compensation was offered. So the model breaks where a price changes the meaning of an act: a gift, a duty, a norm. But it survives where this part has tested it: penalties deter, mostly through the chance of being caught; class size and teachers matter; children respond to their price; smokers respond to theirs. And the reply to the critics was the economic approach itself: put duty, identity and the wish to look good into the model, as Roland Bénabou and Jean Tirole did, and test it. The method was extended, not abandoned.
Frontier: Chapter sixteen. Frontier: fertility and the marriage market.

The first open question is how low fertility will go, and why. Since 1990, children per woman in four large economies. Becker's model predicts a fall as women's time grows dearer, but not this: South Korea, at 0.72 children per woman in 2023, where each generation is about 66 percent smaller than the one before. Governments in East Asia and Europe now pay for births, with limited success. Why the fall is so deep in some rich countries and not others is one of the field's live questions.

The second is a reversal. In 1980, across rich countries, the more women worked, the fewer children were born, as Becker's model of the price of time predicts. Today the relation runs the other way: the rich countries where more women work have more children. Matthias Doepke, Anne Hannusch, Fabian Kindermann and Michèle Tertilt argue that what now matters is whether work and children can be combined: childcare, fathers who share the work at home, flexible jobs, and the norms that govern all three. How much of that policy can change, and how fast, is open.

The third joins the family to the whole economy. Where parents preferred sons, and could choose, more boys than girls were born; in China the one-child policy sharpened it. A generation later, young men outnumber young women, and, as in chapter five's Island with more men, many will not marry. Shang-Jin Wei and Xiaobo Zhang found that parents of sons save more to improve their sons' chances, with a house or wealth, and that families without sons save more too, to keep up. They estimate this can explain about 50 percent of the rise in China's household saving from 1990 to 2007. On the Island, a fifth more men cuts the share of men who marry from 82 to 74 percent. Becker's marriage market, it turns out, reaches into the national accounts and the world's trade balances.
